Possibly constructed by [Leonardo da Vinci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci "Leonardo da Vinci") around the year 1495.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-nih-30)

Among the first verifiable automation is a [humanoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanoid "Humanoid") drawn by [Leonardo da Vinci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci "Leonardo da Vinci") (1452–1519) in around 1495. Leonardo's notebooks, rediscovered in the 1950s, contain detailed drawings of a mechanical [knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight "Knight") in armor which was able to sit up, wave its arms and move its head and jaw.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-nih-30) In the mid-1400s, [Johannes Müller von Königsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_M%C3%BCller_von_K%C3%B6nigsberg "Johannes Müller von Königsberg") created an automaton eagle and fly made of iron; both could fly. [John Dee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dee "John Dee") is also known for creating a wooden beetle, capable of flying.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-BBC-31)

[![Image 7: An illustration showing the inner workings of The Turk automaton, an 18th-century chess-playing machine](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Racknitz_-_The_Turk_3.jpg/250px-Racknitz_-_The_Turk_3.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Racknitz_-_The_Turk_3.jpg)

The secret interior of [The Turk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanical_Turk "Mechanical Turk")

[![Image 8: Vintage doll dressed in ornate robes holding cup](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/KarakuriBritishMuseum.jpg/250px-KarakuriBritishMuseum.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KarakuriBritishMuseum.jpg)

Tea-serving [karakuri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakuri_ningy%C5%8D "Karakuri ningyō"), with mechanism, 19th century. [Tokyo National Science Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_National_Science_Museum "Tokyo National Science Museum").

The 17th-century thinker [René Descartes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Descartes "René Descartes") believed that animals and humans were biological machines. On his last trip to Norway, he took with him a mechanical doll that looked like his dead daughter Francine.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-ReferenceB-32) In the 18th century the master toymaker [Jacques de Vaucanson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_de_Vaucanson "Jacques de Vaucanson") built for [Louis XV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XV "Louis XV") an automated duck with hundreds of moving parts, which could eat and drink. Vaucanson subsequently built humanoid automatons, a drummer and fife player were noted for their anatomical similarity to real human beings.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-33) Vaucanson's creation inspired European [watchmakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watchmaker "Watchmaker") to manufacture mechanical automata and it became fashionable among the European aristocracy to collect sophisticated mechanical devices for entertainment.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-ReferenceB-32) In 1747 [Julien Offray de La Mettrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julien_Offray_de_La_Mettrie "Julien Offray de La Mettrie") anonymously published _[L'homme machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%27homme\_machine "L'homme machine")_ (_Man a Machine_), in which he called Vaucanson a "new [Prometheus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prometheus "Prometheus")" and mused "the human body is a watch, a large watch constructed with such skill and ingenuity".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-34)

In the 1770s the Swiss [Pierre Jaquet-Droz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Jaquet-Droz "Pierre Jaquet-Droz") created moving automata that looked like children, which delighted [Mary Shelley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Shelley "Mary Shelley"), who went on to write the 1818 novel _[Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankenstein;\_or,\_The\_Modern\_Prometheus "Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus")_. The ultimate attempt at automation was [The Turk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanical_Turk "Mechanical Turk") by [Wolfgang von Kempelen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_von_Kempelen "Wolfgang von Kempelen"), a seemingly sophisticated machine that could play [chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess "Chess") against a human opponent and toured Europe. When the machine was brought to the new world, it prompted [Edgar Allan Poe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Allan_Poe "Edgar Allan Poe") to pen an essay, in which he concluded that it was impossible for mechanical devices to reason or think.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-ReferenceB-32) However, The Mechanical Turk was later revealed to be an elaborate hoax: The machine concealed a human, who operated it from the inside.

In the 19th century the Japanese craftsman [Hisashige Tanaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hisashige_Tanaka "Hisashige Tanaka"), known as "Japan's Edison", created an array of extremely complex mechanical toys, some of which could serve tea, fire arrows drawn from a quiver, or even paint a Japanese _[kanji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanji "Kanji")_ character. The landmark text _[Karakuri Zui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakuri\_ningy%C5%8D "Karakuri ningyō")_ (_Illustrated Machinery_) was published in 1796.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-Horn-35) In 1898 [Nikola Tesla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Tesla "Nikola Tesla") demonstrated his "teleautomaton", a prototype remote-controlled boat at [Madison Square Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Square_Garden "Madison Square Garden") as "an automaton which left to itself, will act as though possessed of reason and without any willful control from the outside." He defended his invention against critical reporters, arguing that it was not a "wireless torpedo", but instead, "the first of a race of robots, mechanical men which will do the laborious work of the human race."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-36)

[![Image 9: The cover of the book “The Wonderful Wizard of Oz” by L. Frank Baum, with pictures by W.W. Denslow, shows the Tin Man and the Scarecrow with the Cowardly Lion](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/The_Wonderful_Wizard_of_Oz%2C_006.png/250px-The_Wonderful_Wizard_of_Oz%2C_006.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Wonderful_Wizard_of_Oz,_006.png)

The interior title page of a 1900 _[The Wonderful Wizard of Oz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wonderful\_Wizard\_of\_Oz "The Wonderful Wizard of Oz")_ edition

[![Image 10: Two men, one in a suit, stand at a table that has a complex electronic or scientific device on it](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Gonzalo_showing_El_Ajedrecista_to_Norbert_Wiener.jpg/250px-Gonzalo_showing_El_Ajedrecista_to_Norbert_Wiener.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gonzalo_showing_El_Ajedrecista_to_Norbert_Wiener.jpg)

Gonzalo, Torres Quevedo's son, showing _El Ajedrecista_ to [Norbert Wiener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norbert_Wiener "Norbert Wiener") at the 1951 Paris Cybernetic Conference[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-37)

[![Image 11: Full-length front view of a futuristic humanoid robot with a smooth metallic finish, highlighted by bright green lighting, as it stands on display in a museum setting](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Science_Museum_-_Robots_-_Metropolis_%2833268065925%29.jpg/250px-Science_Museum_-_Robots_-_Metropolis_%2833268065925%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Science_Museum_-_Robots_-_Metropolis_(33268065925).jpg)

The robot Maria from _[Metropolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis\_(1927\_film) "Metropolis (1927 film)")_

Starting in 1900, [L. Frank Baum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L._Frank_Baum "L. Frank Baum") introduced contemporary technology into [children's books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children%27s_books "Children's books") in the Oz series. In _[The Wonderful Wizard of Oz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wonderful\_Wizard\_of\_Oz "The Wonderful Wizard of Oz")_ (1900) Baum told the story of the [cyborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyborg "Cyborg")[Tin Woodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin_Woodman "Tin Woodman"), a human woodcutter who had his limbs, head and body replaced by a tinsmith after his wicked axe had severed them. In _[Ozma of Oz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozma\_of\_Oz "Ozma of Oz")_ (1907) Baum describes the copper clockwork man [Tik-Tok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tik-Tok_(Oz) "Tik-Tok (Oz)"), who needs to be continuously wound up and runs down at inopportune moments.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-38)

In 1903, the Spanish engineer [Leonardo Torres Quevedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_Torres_Quevedo "Leonardo Torres Quevedo") introduced a radio based control system called the "_Telekino_" at the [Paris Academy of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Academy_of_Science "Paris Academy of Science").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-39) It was intended as a way of testing a [dirigible of his own design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astra-Torres_airship "Astra-Torres airship") without risking human lives. Unlike other methods, which carried out 'on/off' actions, Torres established a system for controlling any mechanical or electrical device with different states of operation.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-Yuste2008-40) The transmitter was capable of sending a family of different codewords by means of a binary telegraph signal, and the receiver was able to set up a different state of operation in the device being used, depending on the codeword. The _Telekino_ could execute 19 different commands. In 1905, Torres chose to conduct initial _Telekino_ testing in an electrical three-wheeled land vehicle.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-R._Everett_2015,_pages_91-95-41) In 1906, in the presence of an audience which included the King of Spain, Torres demonstrated the invention in the [Port of Bilbao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Bilbao "Port of Bilbao"), guiding a boat from the shore with people on board, which was controlled at a distance over 2 km.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-42)

In 1912, [Leonardo Torres Quevedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_Torres_Quevedo "Leonardo Torres Quevedo") built the first truly autonomous machine capable of playing chess. As opposed to the human-operated [The Turk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanical_Turk "Mechanical Turk") and [Ajeeb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajeeb "Ajeeb"), _[El Ajedrecista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Ajedrecista "El Ajedrecista")_ (The Chessplayer) had a true integrated automation built to play chess without human guidance. It only played an [endgame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_endgame "Chess endgame") with three [chess pieces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_piece "Chess piece"), automatically moving a white [king](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_(chess) "King (chess)") and a [rook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rook_(chess) "Rook (chess)") to [checkmate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkmate "Checkmate") the black king moved by a human opponent.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-Williams-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-44) In 1951 _El Ajedrecista_ defeats [Savielly Tartakower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savielly_Tartakower "Savielly Tartakower") at the Paris Cybernetic Conference, being the first [Grandmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_(chess) "Grandmaster (chess)") to be defeated by a machine.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-45) In his 1914 paper _Essays on Automatics_, Torres proposed a machine that makes "judgments" using sensors that capture information from the outside, parts that manipulate the outside world like arms, power sources such as batteries and air pressure, and most importantly, captured information and past information. It was defined as an organism that can control reactions in response to external information and adapt to changes in the environment to change its behavior.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-LTQ1914es-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-LTQ1915fr-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-Randell1982p89-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-49)

The term "robot" was first used in a play published by the Czech [Karel Čapek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karel_%C4%8Capek "Karel Čapek") in 1920. _R.U.R._ ([Rossum's Universal Robots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rossum%27s_Universal_Robots "Rossum's Universal Robots")) was a satire, robots were manufactured biological beings that performed all unpleasant manual labor.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-50) According to Čapek, the word was created by his brother [Josef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_Capek "Josef Capek") from the Czech word _robota_ '[corvée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corv%C3%A9e "Corvée")', or in Slovak 'work' or 'labor'.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-51) (Karel Čapek was working on his play during his stay in [Trenčianske Teplice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tren%C4%8Dianske_Teplice "Trenčianske Teplice") in [Slovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia "Slovakia") where his father worked as a medical doctor.) The play _R.U.R,_ replaced the popular use of the word "automaton".[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-52)

[Westinghouse Electric Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westinghouse_Electric_Corporation "Westinghouse Electric Corporation") built Televox in 1926; it was a cardboard cutout connected to various devices which users could turn on and off.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-53) In 1927, [Fritz Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Lang "Fritz Lang")'s [Metropolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis_(1927_film) "Metropolis (1927 film)") was released; the [Maschinenmensch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maschinenmensch "Maschinenmensch") ("machine-human"), a [gynoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gynoid "Gynoid") humanoid robot, also called "Parody", "Futura", "Robotrix", or the "Maria impersonator" (played by German actress [Brigitte Helm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigitte_Helm "Brigitte Helm")), was the first robot ever to be depicted on film.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-MG-54)

The most famous Japanese robotic automaton was presented to the public in 1927. The [Gakutensoku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gakutensoku "Gakutensoku") was supposed to have a diplomatic role. Actuated by compressed air, it could write fluidly and raise its [eyelids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyelids "Eyelids").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-ReferenceA-19) Many robots were constructed before the dawn of computer-controlled servomechanisms, for the public relations purposes of major firms. These were essentially machines that could perform a few stunts, like the automata of the 18th century. In 1928, one of the first humanoid robots was exhibited at the annual exhibition of the Model Engineers Society in London. Invented by W. H. Richards, the robot - named [Eric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_(robot) "Eric (robot)") - consisted of an [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium")[suit of armour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_armour "Body armour") with eleven [electromagnets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnet "Electromagnet") and one motor powered by a 12-volt power source. The robot could move its hands and head and could be controlled by remote control or voice control.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-55)

The earliest designs of [industrial robots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_robots "Industrial robots") were put into production in the United States. These _manipulators_ had [joints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joints "Joints") modelled on human [shoulder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoulder "Shoulder")-arm-[wrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrist "Wrist")[kinetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinetics_(physics) "Kinetics (physics)") to replicate human motions like pulling, pushing, pressing and lifting. Motions could be controlled through [cam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cam_(mechanism) "Cam (mechanism)") and [switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switch "Switch") programming. In 1938 [Willard V. Pollard](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Willard_V._Pollard&action=edit&redlink=1 "Willard V. Pollard (page does not exist)") filed the first patent application for such an arm, the "Position Controlling Apparatus" with electronic controllers, [pneumatic cylinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumatic_cylinder "Pneumatic cylinder") and motors that powered six axes of motion. But the large [drum memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_memory "Drum memory") made programming time-consuming and difficult.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-56)

In 1939, the humanoid robot known as [Elektro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elektro "Elektro") appeared at the [World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World%27s_Fair "World's Fair").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-58) Seven feet tall (2.1 m) and weighing 265 pounds (120 kg), it could walk by voice command, speak about 700 words (using a 78-rpm [record player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_player "Record player")), smoke cigarettes, blow up balloons, and move its head and arms. The body consisted of a steel gear cam and motor skeleton covered by an aluminium skin.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-59)

In 1939 [Konrad Zuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konrad_Zuse "Konrad Zuse") constructed the first [programmable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_program "Computer program") electromechanical [computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer "Computer"), laying the foundation for the construction of a humanoid machine that is now deemed a robot.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-Armin_Krishnan_2016_15-60) The practical application of [binary logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_logic "Boolean logic") to electric switches had been demonstrated by [Claude Shannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon "Claude Shannon"), but his [calculator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculator "Calculator") was not programmable.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-61)

In 1941 and 1942, [Isaac Asimov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Asimov "Isaac Asimov") formulated the [Three Laws of Robotics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Laws_of_Robotics "Three Laws of Robotics"), and in the process coined the word "robotics".[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In 1945 [Vannevar Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannevar_Bush "Vannevar Bush") published [As We May Think](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/As_We_May_Think "As We May Think"), an essay that investigated the potential of [electronic data processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_data_processing "Electronic data processing"). He predicted the rise of computers, digital word processors, [voice recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speech_recognition "Speech recognition") and [machine translation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_translation "Machine translation"). He was later credited by [Ted Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Nelson "Ted Nelson"), the inventor of [hypertext](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertext "Hypertext").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-Robotics_in_Genitourinary_Surgery-18)

[![Image 12: Four men in suits stand in front of a large electronic device, likely a computer, in a black and white photograph](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Julian_Bigelow.jpg/250px-Julian_Bigelow.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Julian_Bigelow.jpg)

[Julian Bigelow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Bigelow "Julian Bigelow") at The Princeton Institute for Advanced Study (left to right: Bigelow, [Herman Goldstine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Goldstine "Herman Goldstine"), [J. Robert Oppenheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Robert_Oppenheimer "J. Robert Oppenheimer"), and [John von Neumann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_von_Neumann "John von Neumann"))

In 1943 [Arturo Rosenblueth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Rosenblueth "Arturo Rosenblueth"), [Norbert Wiener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norbert_Wiener "Norbert Wiener") and [Julian Bigelow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Bigelow "Julian Bigelow") adopted the human [central nervous system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_nervous_system "Central nervous system") as control paradigm for [automatic weapons systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lethal_autonomous_weapon "Lethal autonomous weapon"). In doing so they pioneered [cybernetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cybernetics "Cybernetics") (Greek for _steersman_) and modelled [data processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_processing "Data processing") on the assumption that an animal continually communicates its sensorial experience to its central nervous system as automatic and involuntary feedback, thus being able to regulate processes such as [respiration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiration_(physiology) "Respiration (physiology)"), [circulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circulatory_system "Circulatory system") and [digestion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digestion "Digestion").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-62) Following the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), at a 1946 conference on cybernetics, [Warren McCulloch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_McCulloch "Warren McCulloch") gathered a team of mathematicians, computer engineers, [physiologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiologists "Physiologists") and [psychologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychologists "Psychologists") to work on machine operation using biological systems as starting point. Following the publication of his book in 1948, Wiener's idea that inanimate systems could simulate biological and social systems through the use of sensors led to the adaption of cybernetic theories into industrial machines. But [servo controllers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Servo_control "Servo control") proved inadequate in achieving the desired level of automation.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-63)

The first electronic autonomous robots with complex behavior were created by [William Grey Walter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Grey_Walter "William Grey Walter") of the [Burden Neurological Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burden_Neurological_Institute "Burden Neurological Institute") at Bristol, England in 1948 and 1949. He wanted to prove that rich connections between a small number of [brain cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurons "Neurons") could give rise to very complex [behaviors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Behavior "Behavior") - essentially that the secret of how the brain worked lay in how it was wired up. His first robots, named [Elmer and Elsie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elmer_and_Elsie_(robots) "Elmer and Elsie (robots)"), were constructed between 1948 and 1949 and were often described as "tortoises" due to their shape and slow rate of movement. The three-wheeled tortoise robots were capable of [phototaxis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phototaxis "Phototaxis"), by which they could find their way to a recharging station when they ran low on battery power.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Walter stressed the importance of using purely [analogue electronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analogue_electronics "Analogue electronics") to [simulate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simulate "Simulate") brain processes at a time when his contemporaries such as [Alan Turing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Turing "Alan Turing") and [John von Neumann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_von_Neumann "John von Neumann") were all turning towards a view of mental processes in terms of [digital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_data "Digital data")[computation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computation "Computation"). Walter's work inspired subsequent generations of robotics researchers such as [Rodney Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodney_Brooks "Rodney Brooks"), [Hans Moravec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Moravec "Hans Moravec") and [Mark Tilden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Tilden "Mark Tilden"). Modern incarnations of Walter's "turtles" may be found in the form of [BEAM robotics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BEAM_robotics "BEAM robotics").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-gwonline-64)

In 1949 [Tony Sale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Sale "Tony Sale") built a simple 6-foot (1.8 m) [humanoid robot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanoid_robot "Humanoid robot") he named [George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_(robot) "George (robot)"), created from scrap metal from a grounded [Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vickers_Wellington "Vickers Wellington") bomber. After being stored away in its inventor's shed, the robot was restored in 2010 and shown in an episode of [Wallace & Gromit's World of Invention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_%26_Gromit%27s_World_of_Invention "Wallace & Gromit's World of Invention"). After the reactivation, Tony Sale donated George to the [National Museum of Computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_Museum_of_Computing "The National Museum of Computing"), where it remains on display to the public.

[![Image 13: A worker in a lab coat and protective eyewear stands beside a large industrial robot with a monitor, likely overseeing or controlling its operations](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Computer_Integrated_Manufacturing_Systems%28CMS%29Unimate_Pumo_500_%26_Pumo_560_Robots_1986%282%29.jpg/250px-Computer_Integrated_Manufacturing_Systems%28CMS%29Unimate_Pumo_500_%26_Pumo_560_Robots_1986%282%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Computer_Integrated_Manufacturing_Systems(CMS)Unimate_Pumo_500_%26_Pumo_560_Robots_1986(2).jpg)

The Unimate Puma 500 and Puma 560 [industrial robots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_robots "Industrial robots") in 1986

In 1951 Walter published the paper _A Machine that learns_, documenting how his more advanced mechanical robots acted as [intelligent agent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligent_agent "Intelligent agent") by demonstrating conditioned reflex learning.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-Robotics_in_Genitourinary_Surgery-18)

[Unimate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimate "Unimate"), the first digitally operated and programmable robot, was invented by [George Devol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Devol "George Devol") in 1950 and "represents the foundation of the modern robotics industry."[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-66)

In Japan, robots became popular comic book characters. Robots became cultural icons and the Japanese government was spurred into funding research into [robotics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robotics "Robotics"). Among the most iconic characters was the [Astro Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astro_Boy "Astro Boy"), who is taught human feelings such as love, courage and self-doubt. Culturally, robots in Japan became regarded as helpmates to their human counterparts.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-67)

The introduction of [transistors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor "Transistor") into [computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computers "Computers") in the mid-1950s reduced their size and increased performance. Therefore, computing and programming could be incorporated into a range of applications, including automation.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-68) In 1959 researchers of the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") (MIT) demonstrated computer-assisted manufacturing.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-69)

Devol sold the first Unimate to [General Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Motors "General Motors") in 1960, and it was installed in 1961 in a plant in [Ewing Township, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ewing_Township,_New_Jersey "Ewing Township, New Jersey"), to lift hot pieces of metal from a [die casting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die_casting "Die casting") machine and place them in cooling liquid.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-71) "Without any fanfare, the world's first working robot joined the assembly line at the General Motors plant in Ewing Township in the spring of 1961... It was an automated die-casting mold that dropped red-hot door handles and other such car parts into pools of cooling liquid on a line that moved them along to workers for trimming and buffing." Devol's patent for the first digitally operated programmable robotic arm represents the foundation of the modern robotics industry.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-72)

[![Image 14: A man in a suit and tie stands in a museum next to a exhibit that appears to be some kind of robotic arm or machine on display](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Victor_Scheinman_at_MIT_Museum.agr.jpg/250px-Victor_Scheinman_at_MIT_Museum.agr.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Victor_Scheinman_at_MIT_Museum.agr.jpg)

Victor Scheinman at the [MIT Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIT_Museum "MIT Museum") with a PUMA robot in 2014

The Rancho Arm was developed as a robotic arm to help handicapped patients at the [Rancho Los Amigos Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rancho_Los_Amigos_Hospital "Rancho Los Amigos Hospital") in [Downey, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downey,_California "Downey, California"); this computer-controlled arm was bought by Stanford University in 1963.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-CH-73) In 1967 the first [industrial robot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_robot "Industrial robot") was put to productive use in Japan. The Versatran robot had been developed by [American Machine and Foundry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Machine_and_Foundry "American Machine and Foundry"). A year later a hydraulic robot design by [Unimation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimation "Unimation") was put into production by [Kawasaki Heavy Industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kawasaki_Heavy_Industries "Kawasaki Heavy Industries").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-74)[Marvin Minsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvin_Minsky "Marvin Minsky") created the Tentacle Arm in 1968; the arm was computer-controlled and its 12 joints were powered by hydraulics.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-CH-73) In 1969 [Mechanical Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanical_Engineering "Mechanical Engineering") student [Victor Scheinman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Scheinman "Victor Scheinman") created the Stanford Arm, recognized as the first electronic computer-controlled robotic arm because the Unimate's instructions were stored on a [magnetic drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_drum "Magnetic drum").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-CH-73)

In the late-1960s the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") became the testing ground for automated command technology and sensor networks.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-75) In 1966 the [McNamara Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McNamara_Line "McNamara Line") was proposed with the aim of requiring virtually no ground forces. This sensor network of seismic and acoustic sensors, photoreconnaissance and sensor-triggered [land mines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_mines "Land mines") was only partially implemented due to high cost.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-Armin_Krishnan_2016_20-76) The first mobile robot capable of reasoning about its surroundings, [Shakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakey_the_Robot "Shakey the Robot"), was built in 1970 by the Stanford Research Institute (now [SRI International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SRI_International "SRI International")). Shakey combined multiple sensor inputs, including TV cameras, [laser rangefinders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_rangefinder "Laser rangefinder"), and "bump sensors" to navigate.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-CH-73)

[![Image 15: A military boat being targeted by a falling missile in the middle of the sea](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/GBU-10_shortly_before_it_impacts_a_small_boat_during_a_training_exercise.jpg/250px-GBU-10_shortly_before_it_impacts_a_small_boat_during_a_training_exercise.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GBU-10_shortly_before_it_impacts_a_small_boat_during_a_training_exercise.jpg)

 A [GBU-10 Paveway II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GBU-10_Paveway_II "GBU-10 Paveway II"), an American [laser-guided bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser-guided_bomb "Laser-guided bomb"), based on the [Mk 84](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mk_84 "Mk 84")[general-purpose bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General-purpose_bomb "General-purpose bomb"), but with laser seeker and wings for guidance. Introduced into service c. 1976.

In the early 1970s precision munitions and smart weapons were developed. Weapons became robotic by implementing [terminal guidance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_guidance "Terminal guidance"). At the end of the Vietnam War the first laser-guided bombs were deployed, which could find their target by following a laser beam that was pointed at the target. During the 1972 [Operation Linebacker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Linebacker "Operation Linebacker") laser-guided bombs proved effective, but still depended heavily on human operators. [Fire-and-forget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire-and-forget "Fire-and-forget") weapons were also first deployed in the closing Vietnam War, once launched no further attention or action was required from the operator.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-Armin_Krishnan_2016_20-76)

The development of humanoid robots was advanced considerably by [Japanese robotics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_robotics "Japanese robotics") scientists in the 1970s.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-77)[Waseda University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waseda_University "Waseda University") initiated the WABOT project in 1967, and in 1972 completed the WABOT-1, the world's first full-scale humanoid intelligent robot.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-78) Its limb control system allowed it to walk with the lower limbs, and to grip and transport objects with hands, using tactile sensors. Its vision system allowed it to measure distances and directions to objects using external receptors, artificial eyes and ears. And its conversation system allowed it to communicate with a person in Japanese, with an artificial mouth. This made it the first [android](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Android_(robot) "Android (robot)").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-80)

[Freddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddy_II "Freddy II") and [Freddy II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddy_II "Freddy II") were robots built at the [University of Edinburgh School of Informatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Edinburgh_School_of_Informatics "University of Edinburgh School of Informatics") by [Pat Ambler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Ambler "Pat Ambler"), [Robin Popplestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Popplestone "Robin Popplestone"), [Austin Tate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_Tate "Austin Tate"), and [Donald Mitchie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Mitchie "Donald Mitchie"), and were capable of assembling wooden blocks in a period of several hours.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-81) German based company [KUKA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KUKA "KUKA") built the world's first industrial robot with six electromechanically driven axes, known as FAMULUS.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-82)

In 1974, [Michael J. Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_J._Freeman "Michael J. Freeman") created Leachim, a robot teacher who was programmed with the class curricular, as well as certain biographical information on the 40 students whom Leachim was programmed to teach.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-83) Leachim had the ability to synthesize [human speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_speech "Human speech").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-84) Leachim was tested in a fourth grade classroom in the [Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronx "Bronx") borough of [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-85)

In 1974, David Silver designed The Silver Arm, which was capable of fine movements replicating human hands. Feedback was provided by [touch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touch_sensor "Touch sensor") and [pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressure_sensor "Pressure sensor")[sensors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensors "Sensors") and analyzed by a computer.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-CH-73) The [SCARA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SCARA "SCARA"), Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arm, was created in 1978 as an efficient, 4-axis robotic arm. Best used for picking up parts and placing them in another location, the SCARA was introduced to assembly lines in 1981.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-86)

The Stanford Cart successfully crossed a room full of chairs in 1979. It relied primarily on [stereo vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereo_vision "Stereo vision") to navigate and determine distances.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-CH-73) The [Robotics Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robotics_Institute "Robotics Institute") at [Carnegie Mellon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Mellon_University "Carnegie Mellon University") was founded in 1979 by [Raj Reddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raj_Reddy "Raj Reddy").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-87)

[![Image 16: A robotic car factory building a car chassis](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/KUKA_Industrial_Robots_IR.jpg/250px-KUKA_Industrial_Robots_IR.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KUKA_Industrial_Robots_IR.jpg)

[KUKA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KUKA "KUKA") IR 160/60 Robots from 1983

[![Image 17: Man high-fiving with a robot arm in a laboratory](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Db_tuda_jes2899_a.jpg/250px-Db_tuda_jes2899_a.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Db_tuda_jes2899_a.jpg)

Sensors allow collaborative robots ([cobots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobots "Cobots")) to interact directly with humans in a shared [workspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workspace "Workspace").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-88)

[Takeo Kanade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takeo_Kanade "Takeo Kanade") created the first "direct-drive arm" in 1981. The first of its kind, the arm's motors were contained within the robot itself, eliminating long transmissions.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-89)

In 1984 Wabot-2 was revealed; capable of playing the organ, Wabot-2 had 10 fingers and two feet. Wabot-2 was able to read a score of music and accompany a person.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-90)

In 1986, [Honda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honda "Honda") began its humanoid research and development program to create robots capable of interacting successfully with humans.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-91) A [hexapodal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexapod_(robotics) "Hexapod (robotics)") robot named Genghis was revealed by MIT in 1989. Genghis was famous for being made quickly and cheaply due to construction methods; Genghis used 4 microprocessors, 22 sensors, and 12 [servo motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Servo_motors "Servo motors").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-92) Rodney Brooks and Anita M. Flynn published "Fast, Cheap, and Out of Control: A Robot Invasion of The Solar System". The paper advocated creating smaller cheaper robots in greater numbers to increase production time and decrease the difficulty of launching robots into space.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-93)

In 1994 one of the most successful [robot-assisted surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robot-assisted_surgery "Robot-assisted surgery") appliances was cleared by the [FDA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FDA "FDA"). The [Cyberknife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberknife_(device) "Cyberknife (device)") had been invented by [John R. Adler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_R._Adler "John R. Adler") and the first system was installed at Stanford University in 1991. This [radiosurgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiosurgery "Radiosurgery") system integrated [image-guided surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image-guided_surgery "Image-guided surgery") with robotic positioning. The Cyberknife is now deployed to treat patients with brain or spine [tumors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumors "Tumors"). An [x-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray "X-ray") camera tracks displacement and compensates for motion caused by breathing.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-94)

The [biomimetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomimetic "Biomimetic") robot [RoboTuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RoboTuna "RoboTuna") was built by doctoral student David Barrett at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1996 to study how fish swim in water. RoboTuna is designed to swim and to resemble a [bluefin tuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluefin_tuna "Bluefin tuna").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-95)

[![Image 18: An IBM RS/6000 SP computer on display, featuring a large black cabinet with vertical slots and the IBM logo, resting on a dark blue pedestal in a museum setting](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Deep_Blue.jpg/250px-Deep_Blue.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Deep_Blue.jpg)

[IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM")'s [Deep Blue computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Blue_(chess_computer) "Deep Blue (chess computer)") defeated world chess champion [Garry Kasparov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garry_Kasparov "Garry Kasparov") in 1997.

Honda's [P2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honda_P2 "Honda P2") humanoid robot was first shown in 1996. Standing for "Prototype Model 2", P2 was an integral part of Honda's humanoid development project; over 6 feet (1.8 m) tall, P2 was smaller than its predecessors and appeared to be more human-like in its motions.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-96)

Expected to operate for only seven days, the [Sojourner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sojourner_(rover) "Sojourner (rover)") rover finally shuts down after 83 days of operation in 1997. This small robot (only 23 lbs or 10.5 kg) performed semi-autonomous operations on the surface of [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") as part of the [Mars Pathfinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Pathfinder "Mars Pathfinder") mission; equipped with an obstacle avoidance program, Sojourner was capable of planning and navigating routes to study the surface of the planet. Sojourner's ability to navigate with little data about its environment and nearby surroundings allowed it to react to unplanned events and objects.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-97)

The [P3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honda_P3 "Honda P3") humanoid robot was revealed by Honda in 1998 as a part of the company's continuing humanoid project.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-98) In 1999, Sony introduced the [AIBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIBO "AIBO"), a robotic dog capable of interacting with humans; the first models released in Japan sold out in 20 minutes.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-99) Honda revealed the most advanced result of their humanoid project in 2000, named [ASIMO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASIMO "ASIMO"). ASIMO can run, walk, communicate with humans, recognise faces, environment, voices and posture, and interact with its environment.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-100) Sony also revealed its [Sony Dream Robots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QRIO "QRIO"), small humanoid robots in development for entertainment.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-101) In October 2000, the United Nations estimated that there were 742,500 industrial robots in the world, with more than half of them being used in Japan.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-BBC-31)

[![Image 19: A round-shaped, white iRobot Roomba vacuum cleaner sitting on a wooden floor](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6b/Roomba3g.jpg/250px-Roomba3g.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Roomba3g.jpg)

[Roomba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roomba "Roomba")[vacuum cleaner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum_cleaner "Vacuum cleaner") docked in base station

In April 2001, the [Canadarm2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm2 "Canadarm2") was launched into orbit and attached to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"). The Canadarm2 is a larger, more capable version of the arm used by the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle"), and is hailed as "smarter".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-102) Also in April, the [Unmanned Aerial Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unmanned_Aerial_Vehicle "Unmanned Aerial Vehicle")[Global Hawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Hawk "Global Hawk") made the first autonomous non-stop flight over the Pacific Ocean from [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") in California to [RAAF Base Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAAF_Base_Edinburgh "RAAF Base Edinburgh") in Southern Australia. The flight was made in 22 hours.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-103)

The popular [Roomba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roomba "Roomba"), a robotic vacuum cleaner, was first released in 2002 by the company [iRobot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IRobot "IRobot").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-104)

In 2002, in her book _Designing Sociable Robots,_[Cynthia Breazeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Breazeal "Cynthia Breazeal") was one of the first to explore the idea of robots imitating humans, and published research on how, in the future, teaching humanoid robots to perform new tasks might be as simple as just showing them.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-105) Throughout the early 2000s Breazeal was experimenting with expressive social exchange between humans and humanoid robots. Whilst completing her PhD at [MIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology"), she worked on humanoid robots Kismet, Leonard, Aida, Autom and Huggable.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-106) Doing this, Breazeal found that the issue was that robots too often only interacted with objects and not people and suggested that robots can be used to better relationships between humans.

In 2005, [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University") revealed a robotic system of block-modules capable of attaching and detaching, described as the first robot capable of self-replication, because it was capable of assembling copies of itself if it was placed near more of the blocks which composed it.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-107) Launched in 2003, on 3 and 24 January, the Mars rovers [Spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_(rover) "Spirit (rover)") and [Opportunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_(rover) "Opportunity (rover)") landed on the surface of Mars. Both robots drove many times the distance originally expected, and Opportunity was still operating as late as mid-2018, before communications were lost due to a major dust storm.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-108)

[Self-driving cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-driving_cars "Self-driving cars") had made their appearance by around 2005, but there was room for improvement. None of the 15 devices competing in the [DARPA Grand Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DARPA_Grand_Challenge "DARPA Grand Challenge") (2004) successfully completed the course; in fact no robot successfully navigated more than 5% of the 150-mile (240 km) off-road course, leaving the $1 million prize unclaimed.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-109) In 2005, Honda revealed a new version of its ASIMO robot, updated with new behaviors and capabilities.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-110) In 2006, Cornell University revealed its "Starfish" robot, a four-legged robot capable of self modeling[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] and learning to walk after having been damaged.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-111) In 2007, [TOMY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TOMY "TOMY") launched the entertainment robot, i-sobot, a humanoid bipedal robot that can walk like a human and performs kicks and punches and also some entertaining tricks and special actions under "Special Action Mode".

[![Image 20: A robot is sitting in a red chair](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/ICub_-_Festival_Economia_2018_1.jpg/250px-ICub_-_Festival_Economia_2018_1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ICub_-_Festival_Economia_2018_1.jpg)

_[iCub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICub "ICub")_, humanoid robot built by the [Italian Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Institute_of_Technology "Italian Institute of Technology")

The 2010s were defined by large-scale improvements in the availability, power and versatility of commonly available robotic components, as well as the mass proliferation of robots into everyday life, which caused both optimistic speculation and new societal concerns.

Development of humanoid robots continued to advance; [Robonaut 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robonaut_2 "Robonaut 2") was launched to the International Space Station aboard [Space Shuttle Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery") on the [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133") mission in 2011 as the first [humanoid robot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanoid_robot "Humanoid robot") in space. While its initial purpose was to teach engineers how dextrous robots behave in space, the hope is that through upgrades and advancements, it could one day venture outside the station to help spacewalkers make repairs or additions to the station or perform scientific work.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-112) By the end of the decade, humanoid and animal-like robots were capable of clearing difficult obstacle courses, maintaining balance, and even performing [gymnastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastic "Gymnastic") feats.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-113) However, the vast majority of robotic developments in the 2010s instead saw smaller, more specialized non-humanoid robots become cheaper, more capable, and more ubiquitous.

[Moore's Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore%27s_Law "Moore's Law") and the increasing integration of digital electronic components into lightweight and powerful [systems on a chip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_on_a_chip "System on a chip") allowed for the heavy computation necessary for the operation of a robotic system to be performed by smaller and smaller devices. Many of these advances in chip and sensor technology were driven by the growth and spread of [smartphones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartphones "Smartphones"), which demanded these new components to meet the increasing demands of everyday use.

The cost and weight reductions of these components have resulted in a proliferation of new kinds of special-purpose robots. [Quadcopters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadcopter "Quadcopter"), a novelty at the beginning of the decade, became a ubiquitous platform for robotic systems, featuring autonomous navigation and stabilization and carrying increasingly powerful sensors, including stabilized high definition cameras, radar, and surveying equipment. By the end of the decade, the cost of a robotic quadcopter with [4K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4K_resolution "4K resolution") cameras and autonomous navigation had dropped to within range of hobbyist budgets,[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-114) and companies like [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)") were exploring the use of quadcopters to autonomously deliver freight, though deployment of this systems did not happen on a large scale in the decade.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-115)

The decade also saw a boom in the capabilities of [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence"). Over the course of the 2010s, the capacity of onboard computers used within robots increased to the point that robots could perform increasingly complex actions without human guidance, as well as independently process data in more complex ways. The growth of [mobile data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_data "Mobile data") networks and increasing power of [graphics cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics_cards "Graphics cards") for artificial intelligence applications also allowed robots to communicate with distant [clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_cluster "Computer cluster") in real time, effectively boosting the capability of even very simple robots to include cutting-edge artificial intelligence techniques.

The 2010s also saw the growth of new software paradigms, which allowed robots and their AI systems to take advantage of this increased computing power. [Neural networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_networks "Neural networks") became increasingly well developed in the 2010s, with companies like Google offering free and open access to products like [TensorFlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TensorFlow "TensorFlow"), which allowed robot manufacturers to quickly integrate neural nets that allowed for abilities like [facial recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facial_recognition_system "Facial recognition system") and object identification in even the smallest, cheapest robots.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-116)

The growth of robots in the 2010s also coincided with the increasing power of the [open source software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_source_software "Open source software") movement, with many companies offering free access to their artificial intelligence software. Open source hardware, such as the [Raspberry Pi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raspberry_Pi "Raspberry Pi") line of compact [single board computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-board_computer "Single-board computer") and the [Arduino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arduino "Arduino") line of [microcontrollers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microcontroller "Microcontroller"), as well as a growing array of electronic components like [sensors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensors "Sensors") and [motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motors "Motors") dramatically increased in power and decreased in price over the 2010s. Combined with the drop in cost of manufacturing techniques like [3D printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_printing "3D printing"), these components allowed hobbyists, researchers and manufacturers alike to quickly and cheaply build special-purpose robots that exhibited high degrees of artificial intelligence, as well as to share their designs with others around the world.

[Self-driving cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-driving_cars "Self-driving cars") transitioned from speculative to emergent during the decade. By the end of the decade, most new cars were manufactured with robotic subsystems capable of warning the car's human driver about dangers such as nearby vehicles or potential lane departures.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-117) In 2014, new [Tesla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla,_Inc. "Tesla, Inc.") vehicles were fitted with the computer hardware necessary to eventually support a full autopilot software system, with increasingly autonomous software systems arriving as updates over later years.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-118) By the end of the decade, autonomous driving was possible on large highways, but still required human supervision.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-119)

The growth of robotic capabilities during the decade happened in tandem with the centralization of economic power into the hands of [large multinational tech companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Tech "Big Tech"), which has prompted concerns that the capabilities of these robots could be abused by the companies that make them available to consumers. The acquisition of [Roomba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roomba "Roomba") by [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)") led to concerns from data privacy advocates that data about the interiors of users' homes collected by the robots' sensors and cameras could be stored, shared and analyzed without those users' informed consent.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-120) Likewise, the ubiquity of small flying quadcopters, [home automation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_automation "Home automation"), and facial recognition capabilities by robots has caused serious concerns regarding [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") abuses, including allegations of repression of ethnic minorities in [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-121) and concerns about violations of privacy rights by law enforcement in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States").[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-122) As robotic systems showed the ability to perform more and more tasks once limited to human operators, many [ethicists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethicists "Ethicists") raised concerns that robots operating complex systems may not have the moral or ethical safeguards necessary to ensure public safety.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-123)

Throughout the 2010s, humans continued to examine the nature of their relationships with robots, with trends indicating a general belief that robots were or would become conscious beings deserving of rights, and potential allies or rivals to humans. On 25 October 2017 at the Future Investment Summit in [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh"), a robot called [Sophia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophia_(robot) "Sophia (robot)") and referred to with female pronouns was granted [Saudi Arabian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") citizenship, becoming the first robot ever to have a nationality.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-124)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-tc-125) This has attracted controversy, as it is not obvious whether this implies that Sophia can vote or marry, or whether a deliberate system shutdown can be considered murder; as well, it is controversial considering how few rights are given to Saudi human women.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-126)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-127) Popular works of art in the 2010s, such as HBO's revival of _[Westworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westworld "Westworld")_, encouraged empathy for robots, and explored questions of humanity and consciousness.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-128)

By the end of the decade, commercial and industrial robots were in widespread use, performing jobs more cheaply or with greater accuracy and reliability than humans, and were widely used in manufacturing, assembly and packing, transport, Earth and space exploration, surgery, weaponry, laboratory research, and mass production of consumer and industrial goods.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-129) The growth of the use robots across industry, as well as in the [service sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service_sector "Service sector") and in creative or highly skilled jobs formerly limited to humans, led to fears in the latter part of the decade of mass [technological unemployment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technological_unemployment "Technological unemployment").[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-130)

By the very end of the decade, robotics had started to make advancements on the nanotechnology scale. In 2019, engineers at the University of Pennsylvania created millions of nanobots in just a few weeks using technology borrowed from the mature semiconductor industry. These microscopic robots, small enough to be injected into the human body and controlled wirelessly, could one day deliver medications and perform surgeries, revolutionizing medicine and health.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_robots#cite_note-131)
